sections.heading: Build an equipment routine
sections.body: Knowing what equipment you have, where it is located, and when it was last checked makes home maintenance easier to plan.

sections.heading: Inspection and tune-up are different
sections.body: An inspection provides a general safety and operating review. A tune-up is equipment maintenance performed as appropriate by a qualified service professional.
bullets: Confirm who is responsible for repairs

sections.heading: Bring in the right expertise

bullets: Routine maintenance belongs with a service professional
Emergency odor response begins by leaving
Call 811 before work that disturbs the ground

pages.pageTitle: Safety starts with knowing what to do.
pages.pageSubtitle: Recognize a possible leak, leave quickly, and plan every digging project before the first shovel enters the ground.
pages.pageSummary: A high-clarity safety hub that gives emergency odor steps priority, reinforces 811, and separates urgent action from routine equipment care.
pages.metadataDescription: Learn what to do if you smell natural gas, when to call 800-882-3377, and why every digging project begins with 811.

sections.heading: Smell. Go. Let us know.
sections.body: Natural gas is odorized to smell like rotten eggs or sulfur. If you suspect a leak, leave the building or area immediately. From a safe location, call 800-882-3377 or 911.
bullets: Do not use lights, switches, appliances, or phones inside
Do not search for the source
Keep others away until responders say it is safe

sections.heading: Call 811 before you dig
sections.body: A small yard project can still reach buried utilities. Contact 811 before digging so utility operators can arrange to mark underground lines.
bullets: Wait for the required responses and markings

sections.heading: Keep routine safety routine
sections.body: Know your equipment, keep areas clear, follow manufacturer instructions, and use qualified professionals for installation, maintenance, and repair.
bullets: Keep vents and combustion-air openings clear
Install and maintain alarms as required for the home
Treat unusual odors or equipment behavior seriously

pages.pageSubtitle: If you suspect a natural gas leak, leave immediately and call from a safe location.
pages.pageSummary: A concise emergency instruction page designed for scanning under stress, with the odor line and immediate actions placed above supporting detail.
pages.metadataTitle: Smell Natural Gas? Leave and Call 800-882-3377
pages.metadataDescription: If you smell rotten eggs or sulfur, leave immediately. From a safe location call NW Natural at 800-882-3377 or call 911.

sections.heading: 1. Smell
sections.body: Natural gas is odorized so a leak may smell like rotten eggs or sulfur. You might also hear hissing or notice blowing dirt, bubbling water, or unusual plant damage near a line.
bullets: Do not try to confirm the source
Treat even a faint or uncertain odor seriously

sections.heading: 2. Go
sections.body: Leave the building or area immediately. Move to a safe location away from the suspected leak.
bullets: Do not turn lights or switches on or off
Do not use a phone, appliance, garage-door opener, match, or flame indoors
Do not return until emergency responders say it is safe

sections.heading: 3. Let us know
sections.body: Once you are safely away, call the NW Natural emergency line at 800-882-3377 or call 911. Give the location and describe what you noticed.
bullets: Call from outside and away from the odor
Keep people and pets away from the area

recommendedComponents.contentUse: Smell, Go, and Let Us Know steps

pages.pageSubtitle: One simple step helps protect people, property, and underground utility lines.
pages.pageSummary: A clear 811 planning page covering when to call, what happens after the request, and how to work carefully around utility marks.
pages.metadataTitle: Call 811 Before You Dig | NW Natural
pages.metadataDescription: Contact 811 before planting, fencing, trenching, or any project that disturbs the ground, then wait for utility responses and markings.

sections.heading: Every dig begins with 811
sections.body: Buried utilities may be closer to the surface than expected, and a project does not need to be large to create risk. Contact 811 before the work begins.
bullets: Installing posts, fences, mailboxes, or signs

sections.heading: What happens after you contact 811
sections.body: Provide the location and project details, allow the required planning time, and wait for affected utility operators to respond. The current 811 process and timing should be confirmed for the project location.
bullets: Wait for all required utility responses

sections.heading: Dig carefully around the marks
sections.body: Utility marks show an approximate location, not the exact depth. Follow local tolerance-zone and hand-digging requirements, and stop if you expose or damage a line.
bullets: Use the safest permitted digging method
Do not assume depth from a previous project
If a gas line may be damaged, move away and call 800-882-3377 from a safe location

pages.pageTitle: Turning organic waste into useful renewable energy.
pages.pageSubtitle: Renewable natural gas can capture methane from existing waste streams and prepare it for use in the gas system.
pages.pageSummary: An accessible explanation of renewable natural gas, its sources, processing, system role, and the care required when evaluating projects.
pages.metadataDescription: Learn how renewable natural gas can be produced from organic waste, cleaned for pipeline use, and evaluated as part of a lower-carbon energy pathway.

sections.heading: What renewable natural gas is
sections.body: Organic materials can release biogas as they break down. When that gas is captured, cleaned, and conditioned to meet applicable quality requirements, it can become renewable natural gas.
bullets: Potential sources include landfills, wastewater, farms, and food waste
Processing removes moisture and other constituents
Finished gas must meet required specifications before system delivery

sections.heading: Why waste streams matter
sections.body: Some organic waste sources emit methane as part of normal decomposition. Capturing and productively using that gas can be one tool within a broader emissions-reduction strategy.
bullets: Recover energy from material already decomposing
Create potential partnerships across farms, cities, and industry

sections.heading: Evaluate the full project
sections.body: A credible project considers lifecycle emissions, feedstock practices, local impacts, gas quality, cost, regulation, monitoring, and long-term supply—not just the renewable label.

pages.pageTitle: A practical pathway toward a lower-carbon energy future.
pages.pageSubtitle: Use less. Renew the supply. Keep safety, reliability, and customers at the center of the transition.
pages.pageSummary: A high-level environmental platform built around efficiency, renewable supply, resilient infrastructure, transparent learning, and shared action.
pages.metadataDescription: Explore a practical lower-carbon direction based on energy efficiency, renewable supply, resilient infrastructure, partnership, and measurable progress.

sections.heading: Use less through efficiency
sections.body: The cleanest unit of energy is often the one a home or business does not need to use. Better equipment, buildings, controls, and habits can reduce demand while protecting comfort.
bullets: Help customers understand and manage use
Focus on durable savings rather than short-lived claims

sections.heading: Renew the supply
sections.body: Renewable natural gas and other emerging low-carbon fuels may help reduce the lifecycle emissions associated with delivered energy when projects are carefully sourced, measured, and operated.

sections.heading: Build a resilient transition
sections.body: A durable transition should keep people and communities in view. Reliability, affordability, workforce readiness, infrastructure stewardship, and regional needs all belong in the decision.
bullets: Work across public, private, and community partners

sections.heading: Measure, report, improve
sections.body: Progress deserves clear definitions and consistent measurement. Share what is working, where assumptions changed, and what the next learning agenda should address.
bullets: Update the pathway as evidence improves
